This is the unofficial community guide to Life Simulator Reloaded, a mobile life simulation game where you shape a character from the ground up: age day by day, chase careers, fall into (or out of) trouble, and explore optional paths like fame, crime, and monster hunting. Think of this hub as a table-of-contents for the game — jump to whatever arc you are playing today. New here? Start with Character Creation and Basic Mechanics, then skim Beginner Tips before you reroll your first life.

documents.t: Section What you will find Getting Started Rolling your character, how time and stats work, and mistakes to avoid early. Game Mechanics Deep dives into stats, money, relationships, random events, gems, boosts, and mini-games. Jobs & Careers Employment paths from humble gigs to specialist careers — and how to climb. Crime & Prison Risk, reward, wanted level, doing time, fights, and life behind bars. Monster Hunter Hunting, gear, and content tied to the Monster Hunter path. Quests Story beats, tutorials, and long-form goals that structure your run. Achievements Collectibles and bragging rights across every play style.

Life Simulator Reloaded layers four big themes on top of everyday life simulation: Area Vibe Core Everyday life — home, work, education, health, relationships, and the backbone systems. Crime Illegal work, police heat, prison routines, and the consequences of bad choices. Celebrity Spotlight careers and fame-flavored content for players who want the red carpet. Monster Hunter Supernatural threats, dedicated gear and goals, and combat-flavored progression. Not every run has to touch every path — but the game is richest when you bounce between “normal life” and the wilder tracks.

Character Creation Basic Mechanics Beginner Tips & Common Mistakes Stats Crime overview Monster Hunter Quests overview Achievements overview Spoilers & balance Wiki pages may describe mechanics, locations, and outcomes in detail. If you prefer discovering everything blind, bookmark this site and come back after your first full life. Life Simulator Reloaded is a mobile game; this wiki is a player-focused reference and may lag behind the latest app version.
Celebrity content centers on fame and film releases. Achievements expect you to pursue the actor career path (or other sources of fame the game offers).

Achievement Unlock Tips Difficulty Famous Reach 100 fame Take movie roles, PR events, and fame-positive actions Medium Hall of Fame Reach 200 fame Double down on high-tier roles and publicity Hard Strategy: Fame rises slowly—avoid long prison stretches or scandals that wipe fame unless you are role-playing a comeback.

Achievement Unlock Tips Difficulty First Movie Release your first movie Finish a production cycle as an actor Easy Movie Star Release 10 different movies Vary projects; stay employed long term Hard Progress counts distinct releases—repeating the same project may not advance this if the game treats each title separately; follow career prompts to see what counts.

Each requires you to release a movie of that rarity (better scripts, budgets, and outcomes skew toward higher tiers): Achievement Unlock Tips Difficulty Uncommon Movie Release an uncommon movie Better scripts, skills, or budgets Medium Rare Movie Release a rare movie Higher requirements than uncommon Medium–hard Epic Movie Release an epic movie Late-career gear and stats Hard Legendary Movie Release a legendary movie Top-tier luck and investment Hard

Rush First Movie early for the easy badge. Stack fame actions until 100, then push 200 for Hall of Fame. Grind 10 movies while chasing higher rarities—epic and legendary show up more often with stronger skills and better roles. Difficulty summary: Fame badges are medium time sinks; the full movie ladder is hard because of rarity luck and how long a career needs to run.

Finish The Hunter (second tutorial quest) for basics and gear. Upgrade to tracker level 3, then enter the Dark Forest (Into the Darkness). Clear one of each monster type for Monster Encyclopedia while pushing the tracker to level 5. Farm remaining kills toward 500 and chase legendary encounters last, when your gear and stats are strongest. Overall difficulty: Medium–hard — random encounters and economy gate the late tiers.

Achievements in Life Simulator Reloaded are permanent badges for hitting milestones across life sim, crime, celebrity, and monster hunter content. They are organized in the app by module and theme (social, combat, career, and so on).

Most achievements unlock when you complete a specific action successfully (win a fight, buy a lawyer, release a movie at a certain tier, and similar milestones). Some badges depend on running totals—days alive, fights won, books read, and so on. When you cross the required number, the achievement unlocks once. Some achievements are mutually exclusive with failure outcomes (for example succeeding at a riot versus failing it). Read prompts carefully so you know which path you are on.

Module Examples Core Long life, cooking, romance, weddings, quizzes, boxing, gardening Crime Pickpocket, car theft, prison life, escapes, gang, lawyer Celebrity Fame thresholds, movie counts and rarities Monster Hunter First kills per type, 500 kills, top tracker level, Dark Forest

Play one theme per life — prison, acting, or hunting each need time; mixing goals spreads your attention thin. Use the diary / log — pop-ups often confirm progress toward goals that are not spelled out on screen. Gems — a few crime options (for example hiring a lawyer) cost gems on purpose; save currency if you are collecting those badges. Difficulty labels (used in subpages): Easy = one or two sessions; Medium = needs planning; Hard = long grind or strict requirements. Browse Core, Crime & Prison, Celebrity, and Monster Hunter for detailed walkthroughs.

Confirm the module is enabled and you are not in a blocking situation (for example you are dead, or you are outside prison when trying to earn a prison-only badge). Some badges only count success — failing a mini-game may not move progress forward. Day-based checks often update when a new day starts; sleep or advance time after you think you have met the last requirement. Game updates can change numbers or triggers slightly; if something feels off after a patch, check the in-game achievement list for the latest wording.

documents.t: Illegal actions live in the crime module and usually require you to be in the right location, have enough energy, and pass skill checks, decisions, or mini-games.

The crime skill is the backbone of most illegal actions. Higher skill: Improves success odds on probability-based crimes Unlocks or softens harder variants (e.g. smoother pickpocket runs) Stacks with other relevant skills (e.g. driving for vehicle theft, persuasion where dialogue matters) tip Train crime through repeated attempts and module-specific jobs or actions. Pair it with fitness skills if crimes often end in chases or fights.

Theme What you are doing Risk profile Theft Pickpocket, shoplift-style flows Police attention, fines, wanted days Vehicles Steal / joyride cars High heat; chase decisions if spotted Documents Forgery / fraud-style actions Skill gates; can spike wanted heavily Smuggling Move contraband Often multi-step; failure adds crime days Exact action names and on-screen text appear in-game; this page describes systems, not every button label.

Skill level — directly affects many random chance checks on illegal actions Location & timing — some crimes only appear at night or in specific areas Status — low health/morale can block actions or make fights unwinnable Mini-games / decisions — failures often still apply partial penalties (money loss, injury, extra wanted days) aviso Failed crimes usually add remaining sentence even before arrest. Stacking wanted pressure before you are caught makes prison stays longer.

Reward: money, items, quest progress, achievements, and story beats. Risk: wanted flag, extended sentence, job loss on imprisonment, injuries, and long-term criminal record (see Criminal record). Balance short-term cash against whether you can survive prison if caught — see Prison life.
Criminal record is a persistent counter separate from day-to-day wanted pressure. It summarizes how “heavy” your legal history is across the run.

On first imprisonment for a sentence, the game adds your current remaining sentence into criminal record at the moment you are processed into prison. Longer stacked sentences before capture mean a bigger permanent jump. info Criminal record does not tick down automatically when you leave prison. It is a lifetime ledger, not a second sentence timer.

Concept Relationship Remaining sentence Working clock for wanted / prison time; can hit 0 after release or legal reduction Wanted Clears when remaining sentence is 0 (outside prison) In prison No longer true after release or escape Criminal record Accumulates; long-term stain on your history
documents.s: How it relates to other crime state

documents.t: Exact uses can expand with updates, but design intent is clear: Story weight — repeat offender fantasy; pairs with achievements like extreme sentences (100+ days on intake can flag Public Enemy-style recognition) Module flavor — future jobs, loans, or events can read record severity aviso Do not confuse criminal record with Prison Rep. Rep is inside-prison influence and deactivates when you leave; record stays on the character sheet.

If you care about a “clean” legacy character, avoid stacking crime days before arrest. If you are min-maxing prison content, expect record to spike once you finally go in — plan the rest of your run around being an ex-con narratively.

The Crime module (purchasable game module) layers risk-and-reward illegal activity on top of the core life sim. In Life Simulator Reloaded, crime is not a separate mode: it is woven into locations, skills, decisions, and long-term character state.

Area Examples Street crime Pickpocketing, car theft (GTA-style), smuggling, forgery, and related actions tied to the crime skill Consequences Wanted status, police chases, arrest, sentencing, and prison as a full location loop Prison Dedicated locations (cell, yard, gym, library, chapel, etc.), inmate interactions, fights, mini-games, quests, and Prison Rep info You only experience prison content while you are actively serving a sentence. Your remaining sentence (wanted pressure on the outside, time left on the inside) drives escape pressure before arrest and how long you serve after capture.

Commit crimes or fail risky checks → you gain remaining sentence days and can become wanted. While wanted, travel and police interceptors can trigger chase decisions — escape at home or escape on the road, depending on context. Capture sends you to prison; your stay is tied to remaining sentence, and your criminal record grows when you are first imprisoned. aviso Crime scales with skills and luck but always carries sentence extensions, reputation hits, or forced fights. Plan energy and health before long illegal sessions.
How to commit crimes — actions, crime skill, success factors Wanted system — remaining sentence, reducing days, chases Prison life — locations, daily rules, every major prison action

Prison is a full subsystem: multiple locations, daily skill growth, random events, gem sinks, and several mini-games. This page is the canonical deep dive for doing time efficiently (or escaping).

Entering prison auto-starts all three quests: Survivor, Scholar, and Kingpin. They overlap; order below minimizes friction.

Survivor — passive; just stay alive 10 / 20 / 30 days served in prison (tracked as time inside). Scholar — actively park in library for random finds, letters, chapel, counseling — anything that trains Prison Life toward 50% and stacks books read. Kingpin — needs 3 fight wins, gang formed, and a very high Prison Rep milestone (push rep aggressively late; the quest expects top-tier inside influence). info Survivor milestones tick on days served in prison, not sentence length on paper. You can complete Survivor while working the other two if you do not early-release.
Milestone Goal Serve 10 / 20 / 30 days Time served in prison Play pattern: keep morale healthy (pray, letter, meditate), avoid solitary spirals, and do not riot until you understand the risk.

Stack letter, counseling, gossip interactions, and successful meditate for extra Prison Life growth. aviso If you join a gang, you lose parole, counseling, community service, and the passive good-behavior tick — Scholar is still doable, but slower if you needed those crutches.

After gang unlock, gang meetings every 2 days spike rep quickly. Successful riot middle band grants +25 rep (but riot is once and risky). tip Complete Scholar books before going all-in on gang (optional). Kingpin wants social investment anyway — align friendship grinding with gang requirements.

Your character tracks several crime-related pieces of state at once: Concept Role Wanted You are actively sought; interceptors and police events can fire Remaining sentence Pressure from crimes and judgments; drives how long you serve in prison In prison You are serving time in the crime module’s prison loop Criminal record Long-term tally that grows when sentenced; see Criminal record

When illegal outcomes add sentence time (success or failure): Remaining sentence goes up by that many days If you were not wanted and not already in prison, you become wanted and the game logs your first wanted entry If you were already wanted (but not in prison), logs show escalation If you are already in prison, your judgment extends in place

The game can subtract from your remaining sentence (never below zero). When remaining sentence hits zero, wanted clears automatically. info Items or story effects that “reduce your sentence” on the outside use the same remaining-sentence pool. Time served in prison also eats those days day by day until release.

Travel friction — crime module interceptors can trigger when you change location (home vs road variants) Stress on stats — chases and failed escapes hit health, morale, or energy Prison — capture applies your stacked remaining sentence as the baseline for your stay

When police pressure triggers during movement, the game may offer decision checks: Escape at home — chase resolution when the situation is home-adjacent Escape on the road — chase resolution in open travel Success lets you slip away; failure typically deepens the situation (more days, injury, or arrest paths depending on context). aviso Do not treat wanted as “free” debuff time. Every extra chunk of crime time stacks remaining sentence, which becomes real prison time if you are caught.

Specialist electives (any path): leadership, public speaking, self defense, financial literacy, cooking masterclass, survival basics, digital marketing, meditation — patch weak skills for promotions or risky events. tip Public speaking is the best multi-career buy if you rotate through waitress, bartender, or actor.

Driving license if you need quick employable income. One apprenticeship matching your chosen job (mixology, cook, software, economics, acting). Specialist electives only to fix skills you fail in decisions or interviews. tip Do not enroll in gourmet or secure driving until the prerequisite course is fully done — partial progress never satisfies a promotion’s required course.

Education is how you raise skill ceilings faster than job experience alone. In Life Simulator Reloaded, courses cost money, take in-game days, and apply daily skill gain toward a max level cap for that enrollment.

Category What it represents Typical use School Childhood fundamentals Boost academics and school success early Apprenticeship Trade-style intro programs First rung for bartender, cook, developer, acting, economics College Advanced programs Unlocks senior job ranks; often requires the apprenticeship twin Specialist Focused electives Deep dives: driving, self-defense, persuasion workshops, gourmet cooking tip Read listed requirements like a tech tree: if a college course names another course as prerequisite, finish that course before you burn days expecting progress.

Hard gates: Some promotions require finishing a specific course—no certificate, no title. Soft power: Even without a hard gate, higher skills pass decisions and interviews that gate pay bumps. Calendar cost: Each active course consumes days; stack courses sequentially, not in parallel, unless the game lets you focus on more than one at a time (usually one at a time).

Cheap short courses (school, beggar survival) buy optionality early. Mid-price apprenticeships (cook, bartender mixology) pay back quickly if that job is your income core. Expensive specialist/college tracks (gourmet, secure driving, professional acting) are long-run investments—fund them with delivery or mid-tier service work. tip You can accelerate some education spends with gems when the game offers it—save gems for the longest programs if you are impatient, not for courses you can finish in a week of play.
Pick one economic vertical (food, tech, finance, fame) and align every course purchase to that vertical for the first in-game year. Generalists are fun but slower to hit the flashy promotions.

Life Simulator Reloaded runs on a simple loop: choose where to be, do things that cost time and resources, survive the day, and come back tomorrow with new events and opportunities. Here is how that loop fits together.

A “day” is the main unit of progress. When you end a day (or the game advances time): Your character ages along the calendar (20 in-game days = 1 in-game year). Daily hooks fire across items, locations, quests, and modules — this is where diseases heal, rent comes due, prison sentences tick, and story beats trigger. Think in days, plan in years Short-term: “Can I afford food and sleep today?” Long-term: “Where do I want my skills and relationships by next year?”

Piece Role Locations Places you travel to — home, work hubs, shops, special areas (hospital, police station, etc.). Where you stand decides which actions appear. Actions Things you do at a location: work shifts, study, socialize, commit crimes, use items — often tied to skills, money, and risk. Events Questions, decisions, and random encounters that pop up as you play. Some are harmless flavor; others reshape money, relationships, or legal status. You will also meet NPCs, build relationships, buy and use items, take courses, and apply for jobs — all through this location + action lens.
Three vital statuses track whether you can keep going: Status Starting current Max Health 75 100 Energy 75 100 Morale 75 100
If any one of health, energy, or morale hits 0, you die. Treat all three as hard loss conditions.

When any of these stats falls to 20 or below, you are in danger — the game treats this as critically low. Expect worse outcomes from risky actions and prioritize recovery (rest, food, medical help, morale fixes). Zero is game over Do not tank one bar to “save” another. A dead genius is still dead.

Many actions resolve through mini-games — short skill checks (timing, memory, reflex, etc.) that stand in for pickpocketing, lockpicking, fights, interviews, and more. Success usually grants the full reward; failure may waste time, money, or stats. Practice matters: higher relevant skills and smart prep (items, location, rest) tilt odds in your favor. See Mini-games for a full catalog and tips.

Gems are the premium currency. Typical uses include: Skipping or softening difficult mini-games. Boosting tough decisions when failure is expensive. Accelerating certain time-gated or grindy paths (education, recovery, etc., depending on content). Spend gems like a lifeline, not confetti Save them for high-stakes checks — promotions you have waited for, prison survival, rare quest branches — not every minor failure.

Core supplies the baseline loop above. Crime, Celebrity, and Monster Hunter add locations, actions, items, and quests that plug into the same day pass and stat rules — with extra risk/reward on top. Next: Beginner Tips · Stats · Gems & boosts

You do not need a perfect build to enjoy Life Simulator Reloaded — you need habits that keep your character alive long enough for the cool stuff to happen. This page collects practical tips and classic mistakes we see in community runs.

Health, energy, and morale each have a maximum of 100 and a danger threshold around 20. If any bar hits 0, you die. Tip Why it matters Keep all three above 20 when possible Below that, you are fragile; at 0, the run ends. Visit the hospital when health is low Treat early — waiting for a “free” recovery often costs more in lost days and events. Sleep, eat, and fix morale deliberately Energy and morale are not “nice to have”; they are survival stats. The death spiral Players often ignore morale or energy because health still looks “okay.” One bad night plus one bad event can zero a bar. Check all three before risky actions.
documents.s: Stay out of the danger zone

documents.t: Take courses to raise skills that gate jobs you want — especially if your intelligence is average or low (every bit of learning speed helps). Pick one early career target instead of dabbling in ten skills at once; depth unlocks income and new actions sooner. Stack bonuses Combine education, job practice, and safe daily routines so skill XP is not fighting constant stat drain.

Tip Detail Get a job ASAP Even entry-level work stabilizes food, rent, and travel — savings melt fast without income. Do not spend every coin on vibes Items and impulse buys are fun, but cash buffer saves you when RNG taxes you. Save gems for important decisions Use premium currency on high-impact checks: brutal mini-games, quest branches you care about, or recovery moments that salvage a run. Spending gems on noise Burning gems to skip every minor inconvenience leaves you broke when a promotion, trial, or prison event actually needs them.

Complete tutorial quests first — they teach navigation, actions, and systems that the rest of the game assumes you know. Read quest text when stuck: milestones often hint at location, item, or skill requirements.

Build relationships early — friends and partners unlock events, gifts, and support that pure grind cannot replace. Balance social spend with stat upkeep; a packed social calendar on empty energy is how accidents happen.

Mistake Better habit Ignoring health until the UI screams Check health after fights, illness, cheap food streaks, and crime — fix problems at yellow, not red. Blowing all money on day one Keep a multi-day buffer for rent, travel, and emergencies. Never training skills Jobs and quests gate on skills; schedule courses like appointments. Skipping energy/morale recovery Treat rest and fun as maintenance, not optional fluff. Crime without a plan Crime & Prison content is viable — but wanted level and jail time are real progression taxes. Read Crime overview before cosplaying a mastermind. When you lose a run Death is data. Note which bar hit 0 and what you did the day before — that pattern is usually the lesson.

Every new life in Life Simulator Reloaded begins with a few hidden dice rolls and a lot of player choice afterward. This page covers what you start with and how those numbers push your story.
You pick identity basics (like name, gender, country, and appearance) in the app. The game also rolls starting core stats that matter for jobs, learning, and survival — see below.

When a new character is created, the game assigns: Stat Starting range Maximum (typical cap) Intelligence 20–100 (random) 200 Looks 20–100 (random) 200 Reroll regret You cannot “undo” bad luck on day one without starting a new game. If you care about min-maxing, know that both stats can be improved over a long life — but a strong roll still accelerates early progression.

Intelligence influences how fast you learn skills. The higher your intelligence, the quicker you gain levels from courses, jobs, and practice — especially useful when you are juggling many skills at once.

Looks influences how demanding jobs feel on paper. Better looks slightly ease the skill expectations some careers have, which can open doors sooner or make promotions feel less grindy. It is not a substitute for training, but it helps alongside real skill growth.

Concept How it works Starting money Every new character currently begins with 50 cash (same for all runs; a future update could change this). Age & time You start at the beginning of the life timeline. Each in-game year lasts 20 days in real play sessions — the calendar advances as days pass. Day-by-day play You live one day at a time: actions, travel, jobs, and events consume time and move the story forward. Why “20 days = 1 year”? The game compresses childhood and adulthood so decades of life fit a mobile session. When this wiki says in-game years and days, it means that compressed calendar, not real-world calendar years.

Lean into your roll: high intelligence → prioritize courses and skill-heavy jobs early; high looks → you can job-hunt aggressively while you train gaps. Plan your first job: even a modest wage beats burning savings; use early income for food, rest, and stability. Do not neglect “boring” stats: health, energy, and morale still decide whether you live long enough to enjoy high intelligence or looks — see Basic Mechanics. Tutorial quests first: they teach flows (travel, actions, decisions) and often pay rewards that smooth the early curve. Stats are not everything Random events, relationships, crime, and extra content packs can pivot a run hard. A “weak” character with good habits often outlasts a gifted one played recklessly. Illnesses are tracked per save: you can have several active at once. Each night, the health system: Deals damage for every active illness (how hard it hits depends on your age and how severe that disease is) Rolls for a cure if a doctor has identified what you have May add new diseases based on age-weighted chances

New conditions are picked from illnesses you do not already have. Risk goes up with: Age — older characters face higher chance and often worse symptoms Per-disease tuning — some bugs are simply rarer or meaner than others When you catch something, you usually get a popup message specific to that illness.

Each active illness is tracked until it is cured. The game remembers whether a doctor has diagnosed it. Until you are under proper medical identification, automatic nightly cure rolls do not run (except for the witch potion shortcut below).

Path What happens See a doctor At a hospital or prison clinic: the doctor marks every current illness as diagnosed so cure rolls can start Daily cure chance After diagnosis, each night the game rolls a per-disease cure chance; success removes that illness Witch potion A usable item from the witch house — clears your whole active illness list right away (often gem-priced in the market) info The prison clinic uses the same see doctor style care as the city hospital — you are not locked out of diagnosis while sentenced.

Visit a hospital soon after you keep getting sick prompts — untreated illnesses stack their nightly damage. If you are broke, try to rebuild money before bad luck stacks illness on top of job loss. The witch potion is a panic button with a gem cost; compare to Hospital vs witch. aviso Illness damage scales with age. Long lives need regular doctor visits, not “I’ll tough it out one more day.”
Both locations address health crises, but through different economy and risk models. Core gives you science at the hospital and occult commerce at the witch house.

Pros Cons See doctor action diagnoses all active diseases at once Requires travel to hospital location Enables daily cure rolls per disease after care Cure is probabilistic — may take several days Works in prison clinic identical action Does not instantly wipe diseases Best for: early/mid game, steady income, role-play “normal” lives, and prisoners (clinic access). tip If you are danger (≤20 on a meter), detour to hospital before stacking risky actions — doctor flagging is free aside from travel time.

Pros Cons Potion item can instantly clear every disease Expensive — money and/or gem listing No waiting for nightly cure RNG Requires witch location access + inventory space Thematic stat / crafting hooks Less integrated with insurance-like gameplay fantasy Best for: emergency clears before a fight, job interview day, or travel you cannot delay. aviso Relying on witch gems every illness is a hard-currency sink. Hospital care is cheaper long-term if you can afford the time.

Your character has three status meters: health, energy, and morale. Each has a current and maximum value; actions, diseases, jobs, and events raise or lower current.

Rule What it means in play Danger If any of the three meters is 20 or below, you are in danger — the game warns you Death If any meter hits 0 or below, your character dies aviso Because any meter can kill you, a morale crash is as deadly as physical harm. Prison taunts, job-loss spirals, and riot failures can all lead to a “quiet” game over.

Meter Typical drains Typical recovery Health Disease, fights, accidents, bad food Hospital, rest, some items Energy Work, training, travel Sleep, food, some events Morale Repeated failure, hate, isolation Social actions, hobbies, chapel tip Before heavy crime or prison arcs, try to keep each meter comfortably above 20 so one bad day does not drop you straight into danger.

Diseases — ongoing health drain; see Diseases Healing locations — Hospital vs witch Revival — rare story beats can bring you back after a death-like outcome in special cases Watch danger often if you are wanted or hunting — both loops like to chip away at more than one meter at a time.

Books and readable items are a steady path to intelligence, skill ticks, and morale swings. They appear in the market, library, and special vendors; some are single-use while others are flavor logs with stat effects.
Many books push intelligence or academics—ideal for students and white-collar careers. Stack reading with school and courses for faster promotion gates.

Skill-specific manuals (or generic “improvement” reads) grant targeted skill progress. Match the book to your planned job: cooking tomes for chefs, crime manuals for illegal playstyles (where offered). Public library visits and market restocks rotate what is easy to buy—check both when min-maxing.

Prison adds morale reads (magazines, diary writing) and prison life training through written routines. The prison scholar achievement rewards dedicated study behind bars—pair books with safe yard days. tip Read during low-risk days when energy is cheap—books rarely outperform a paid work shift for money, but they compound across decades. In prison, the diary mixes morale and prison life for efficient sentence use.
Items overview Prison items Some books are gag items with big morale swings; check effects before reading in critical moments.

Electronics cover phones, computers, radios, and gadgets that unlock connectivity, career actions, or crime utilities. Many are passive (carry to enable features); some are usable with charges or risk.

Regular and specialty phones may enable calls, social shortcuts, or crime perks (for example, untraceable or smuggled variants tied to risk). Prison phones are powerful but can trigger searches, confiscation, or extra sentence—treat them as high-stakes tools, not toys.

Computers (often paired with internet effects) unlock developer work, computer skill training, and digital side content. Buy them when you commit to tech careers; they are poor impulse purchases for a purely manual job path.

Radios, police scanners, and similar items skew toward morale, information, or evasion bonuses. Expect trade-offs—confiscation chances in restricted areas, decay, or ongoing money costs. When an item description mentions easier escape or witness reduction, it is usually aimed at crime arcs rather than everyday convenience. tip Align electronics with your job: developers want a stable computer + internet stack; criminals may prioritize black-market phones. Do not carry smuggled prison phones during heavy shakedown weeks unless you have a stash or accept the sentence risk.
Items overview Prison items Gem-priced electronics are optional accelerants; core story content is usually reachable without them.

Food and drinks are the most common consumables: they patch your status meters after work, travel, fights, or illness. They are sold at the market, restaurant, bar, and module-specific vendors (e.g. prison canteen items).

Typical effect Why it matters Health Recovery after damage, disease, or risky actions Energy Fuel for daily actions; running empty blocks productivity Morale Mental stability; at 0 morale you can die like health/energy Some items skew heavily toward one meter (snacks for morale, water for health); combo meals spread smaller gains across two or three meters. Read each item’s effect before eating during a crisis—you might need morale more than health.

The crime module adds prison rations-style items (toast, ramen, chocolate, coffee) tuned for cheap meter recovery behind bars. They are ideal for stretching a sentence without gem spending. tip Keep meters above 20 when possible—that band avoids many “danger” outcomes. Carry one morale snack even on money-tight runs; morale crashes end runs as surely as health drops. Alcohol or risky consumables may trade short-term morale for long-term penalties—check logs and effects.

Monster Hunter gear is sold at the Hunter’s Guild and gun shop, with support consumables at the hospital and witch vendors. Your gear works together with aiming, monster lore, and a daily chance to spot monsters around the city.

Buy once at the Hunter’s Guild for 300 (while you are there and you do not already own one). It starts at level 1. Each day (when you are not in prison), the game checks whether a monster is detected at a random public location. What raises your daily detection chance Tracker level — higher levels give a noticeably better chance to find something each day. The jump from level to level is a bit stronger at lower levels than at the top. Hunter’s amulet — wearing it adds a flat bonus to that daily chance. Monster lore — your skill in this area adds a small extra on top, so training lore helps a little every day.

At the guild, each upgrade costs five times your current tracker level in total materials, taken from zombie eyes and bone fragments (eyes are used first until the cost is covered). The tracker caps at level 5. At level 3 you can detect witches and see related map cues; at level 5 you can detect demons and that ties into related achievements. Life Simulator Reloaded uses items for survival (food, medicine), progression (books, training tools), combat (weapons, ammo), careers (electronics, uniforms), and module-specific fantasy (prison contraband, hunting gear, mystery rewards).

Items are grouped in the UI by category labels (food, drinks, weapons, electronics, books, tools, drugs, hunting, etc.). Categories help you browse the market and understand effects at a glance—always read the effect text before bulk-buying.

Most legal goods appear at the market, specialty shops (gun shop, electronics, hospital, Hunter’s Guild), or job-related vendors. Some items are prison-only, black market, or gem-priced. Prices and availability can depend on location, privileges, and whether you already own a unique piece (one-per-character flags).

Usable items are spent or triggered from inventory: they may restore health, energy, or morale, grant skill or stat progress, or start interactions (phone calls, quests). Passive items apply while carried—training gear, trackers, reputation belts. A few items risk confiscation or breakage; see Prison items and Hunting items. Gems can shortcut some purchases; treat them as emergency budget, not your primary grocery money. tip Before long trips or crime sprees, fill cheap stackables (food, drinks) and one emergency consumable. Unique tools (blueprints, trackers) are better bought once at the right location than panic-purchased mid-crisis.

Prison items come from the prison market (canteen), crafting, gems, or fight rewards. They manage meters, reputation, fights, and escape attempts. Several are contraband: guards can shake you down; failing the hide minigame costs items and adds sentence.

Smuggled phone — 10 gems (no cash price). Enables outside calls; ~3%/day confiscation roll that adds 5 days if caught. Shiv — not sold; craft in prison (achievement Craftsman). Weaker than the bought knife but free if you have the route.

Champion belt — earned by beating the champion after 5 prison fight wins (one-time event). Passively grants +3 prison reputation per day. Guard uniform — helps escape attempts; treated as contraband like shiv/phone during shakedowns. It is not on the standard canteen list—watch prison events and content updates for how yours appears. tip First purchases: ramen/coffee for sustain, diary for prison life, then stash if you run contraband. Save blueprint for when you are actively escaping. Delay the gem phone until you accept sentence risk or have stash protection. Confiscation and sentence numbers come from game logic and may be tuned in patches.

Special items are rare, unique, or event-gated pieces: mystery boxes, lucky trinkets, quest rewards, and gem exclusives. They often break normal pricing rules and can trigger random or location-based bonuses.
Mystery purchases trade predictable cash for variance—you might pull consumables, gear, or flavor logs. Budget only surplus money; never bet rent money on boxes unless you are role-playing chaos.
Lucky items sometimes fire on day pass or location change, granting money, mood bumps, or odd encounters. Keep them equipped (carried) for passive proc rates; selling too early loses long-tail value.

Story milestones award non-market items (trophies, keys, module artifacts). These often enable new actions or achievements—read the effect line immediately when you receive one. Duplicate protection is common: if the shop says you already own something, the game is steering you toward a different sink. tip If an item description mentions “while carried”, assume it needs inventory space every day you want the bonus. Rotate specials when you swap life phases (e.g. drop luck charms when entering prison where contraband rules apply).
Items overview Hunting items Drop tables and gem offers can shift between app versions.
Weapons let you fight NPCs, survive prison, and (with the Monster Hunter module) hunt supernatural enemies. They range from improvised shivs to firearms with ammo economies.

Rifles and handguns (where available) consume ammo per use. In hunts, rifles can rarely break—budget replacement cost and keep spare ammo before long trips. Buy ammo at the gun shop or earn it from drops.

Knives, chainsaws, silver daggers, and prison shivs fill melee niches. Prison gear is tuned for inmate fights; hunting daggers add type bonuses (e.g. skeletons). Shivs are often crafted rather than purchased. Always verify an attack is available in your current fight UI—missing ammo or a broken gun silently removes options.

Using weapons in the wrong context raises crime, heat, or search risk. Store or sell contraband before predictable checks when the story allows. tip For monster hunting, bring both ranged and melee options: rifles for raw damage, daggers/chainsaws for skill training and type matchups. For prison, a shiv or knife wins fights faster than bare fists—pair with fighting skill grinding.
Items overview Hunting items Weapon availability depends on module, location, and story state.

The acrobat career is performance plus risk: juggler openings, balance acts, fire dancing, and master acrobat prestige. Sports is the backbone stat, and the job’s interview questions already warn you that injuries are part of the gig.

Sports — trains every day and gates each promotion tier. Some events still test morale and health because tricks fail loudly. tip Before you sign up, bank extra health and energy—failed stunt decisions can chunk your bars. The career is unforgiving if you live permanently in the “danger zone” thresholds.

Acrobat work opens acrobatic movement decisions: choose flashy routines, safe rehearsals, or crowd-pleasing risks. Success spikes pay and fame-style feelings; failure sends you toward hospital visits or lost wages.
Expect questions about injury, teamwork, and motivation. The game treats acrobat hiring like casting for a circus: confidence matters, but reckless answers can backfire in subtle ways.

Start only after teen sports jobs or gym habits raised sports ~30+. Alternate risky shows with rest days so random injuries do not chain. Exit gracefully into actor if you want performance without physical pain. tip If you chase achievements tied to stunt survival, save gems for boosts on the hardest acrobat decisions—those checks are classic gem sinks.

The actor job lives in the celebrity module: acting skill progression, looks and intelligence stat gates, and a visible fame dynamic stat that tracks how known you are. It is the cleanest “become famous” career if you commit to film logic.

Acting — trained on the job and through acting courses. Looks gates many ranks (camera-ready requirements). Intelligence matters for voice work and early tiers. tip Finish acting starter before you expect background or supporting roles. Several levels hard-require the starter course via course requirements—talent alone is not enough.
Fame rises from employment hooks and celebrity events. Higher fame unlocks better pay, stranger random encounters, and more decision pressure (paparazzi, scandals, luxury problems).
Apprenticeship acting — affordable entry, raises skill ceiling for junior roles. Professional acting (college tier) — expensive, requires starter completion, pushes you toward lead-tier fantasy.

Alternate work with morale care; rejection events exist even when you are famous. Invest in public speaking or communication courses if interviews feel harder than performances. Plan money for styling items or looks boosts if promotions stall on stat checks. tip Actor is module-gated—enable celebrity content in your run before you roadmap this path, or you will not see the job at all.

Bankers sit at the bank and climb a long finance ladder: money sorter and cashier early, mortgage and management mid-game, and executive heights for patient players. The defining skill is economics, backed by formal education.

Economics — required at every meaningful promotion; grows from courses and job experience. Soft skills like communication help indirectly in customer-facing bank events, but the hard gates are economic. tip Complete economics apprenticeship before you dream of college economics. The college program requires the apprenticeship certificate—same pattern as developer, different skill.

Apprenticeship economics — moderate price, ~two in-game months, caps skill at a trainee-friendly ceiling. College economics — higher price and duration, raises the ceiling toward manager roles. Bank pay scales slowly at first; you are paying for late-game title jumps, not day-one riches.
Expect paperwork, client advice, and occasional ethical decisions about loans or VIP clients. Good choices lean on economics checks; bad ones hit morale or reputation style outcomes.

Fund courses with delivery or school jobs if you start from zero cash. Raise intelligence for faster skill absorption if you plan multiple finance degrees later. Stack financial literacy (persuasion-adjacent) only if you want cross-career negotiation perks. tip Banker pairs well with developer lives only sequentially—both demand long schooling. Pick one white-collar fantasy per character unless you enjoy slow-burn saves.

Bartenders work the bar location: high mixology demand, steady communication growth, and a strong tip economy driven by random shift events. It is one of the clearest “service plus craft” loops in the game.

Mixology — primary craft stat; gates every promotion after the entry level. Communication — customer handling, drunk patrons, and many event branches. Calmness can appear when you de-escalate instead of brawling. tip The mixology course is not optional for the mid ladder: master bartender expects that training. Buy and finish it before you camp the bar expecting a promotion.

While employed, the game tends to move you to the bar for workdays. Shifts increment cocktails served (with variance), train mixology, and sometimes communication. Random events fire often—tips, recipe quizzes, trouble customers, and occasional fights.

Typical milestones include: Serve 100 cocktails — comes naturally from working; tracks with service statistics. Promote to master bartender — proves you cleared the rank and course gates. Earn 300 in tips — cumulative tips from bar life (event-driven). Reward money helps you pivot to another career or fund education. tip Tips are event-driven. If the quest stalls, keep working and favor tip-friendly event choices when skills allow—do not only wait for base wages.
Stack communication early so drunk-customer and rush events hurt less. Keep health and energy out of the danger zone; bar fights and bad shifts punish low pools hard.

The beggar path is a full street-life career: you earn outside conventional employers, train persuasion and survive in streets, and face a constant stream of random events and decisions—including the infamous pickpocket branch with high risk and high drama.

Survive in streets — resilience to weather, hunger, and trouble; rises from daily work and street events. Persuasion — better outcomes when begging, negotiating, or talking your way out of problems. Fighting and sports show up in chase and conflict options tied to street events. tip Treat survive in streets as your defensive stat and persuasion as your income engine. If both lag, you will fail skill checks on decisions long before you starve.

When you take the job, the Beggar Career quest can track three milestones: Beg 100 times — grind the beg action and daily flow until the counter hits the target. Become district leader — promote through job levels until you hold district leader rank. Earn 500 total from begging — cumulative income from begging-related earnings (tracked for the quest). Completing the arc pays a lump cash reward and marks you as someone who mastered the district.

Beggar life is decision-heavy: turf disputes, police patrols, gang pressure, and pickpocket opportunities. Success can spike morale and money; failure can drain health, morale, and cash. Read skill requirements before you tap the risky option. tip If you are saving for a clean exit from the street, avoid high-variance decisions until you have a cushion. Pickpocket is a story moment—not a stable salary.

Street-focused courses (street survival workshop, persuasion training) accelerate the same skills interviews and promotions expect. They are cheap compared to college tracks and pair well with this career.

The cook (culinary) track is the back-of-house restaurant career: you start in dishwashing and cleaning-heavy roles, then climb toward line cook, pastry, and executive-style titles as cooking and related skills climb.

Cooking — the star of the ladder; promotions and better plates depend on it. Cleaning matters heavily at the bottom ranks (dish pit reality). Leadership and mixology can appear at fancier tiers where the kitchen interfaces with service or specials. tip If you hate the dish pit, rush the basic cooking apprenticeship early. It is inexpensive and moves you toward levels that actually train cooking every day instead of only cleaning.

You are tied to the restaurant flow: expect questions and decisions about ingredients, timing, and pressure during service. Good answers convert to morale, skill bumps, or small bonuses; bad ones tax energy and mood.

Pair the job with cooking courses: a short apprenticeship-style course unlocks fundamentals, while gourmet or masterclass tracks raise the ceiling for late promotions. Specialist-tier cooking programs are pricey—save during mid ranks.

Take cook when you can tolerate energy swings; rush hours hurt if you are already depleted. Alternate work with rest or cheap morale fixes until cooking income stabilizes. Plan one big specialist course before you aim at celebrity-chef fantasy levels. tip Restaurant careers synergize with waitressing if you want to see both sides of the house—but juggling two jobs is slower than finishing one ladder first.

Delivery drivers move goods (and sometimes stranger cargo) for driving-skill pay. It is a practical career for players who want fast employment, vehicle fantasy, and a bridge into secure commercial driving without a college degree.

Driving — the entire ladder; promotions ask for ever-higher mastery. Physical stats indirectly help chase events, but the job checks driving first. tip Enroll in driving license training the moment you hit minimum age. Without it, you are guessing at skill growth instead of compounding daily course gains plus work gains.

Two specialist-style courses stack: Driving license — foundational, shorter, cheaper. Secure driving — advanced, longer, pricier; requires the license course. Finish both before you expect elite delivery titles or weapon-bank style routes that assume professional competence.
Shifts combine driving checks, time pressure, and occasional decisions about shortcuts or suspicious packages. Riskier branches pay better when you succeed; crashes or tickets hurt money and morale.

Keep energy high—long routes punish tired characters. If you use delivery only as a funding job, stop after license + one promotion tier and pivot tuition to developer or banker. Pair with mechanic fantasies only if you enjoy repair side content in other systems. tip Delivery is the best “pay for school” job: strong wages relative to education time, minimal social interview pressure compared to bartender or actress tracks.

The developer track is the flagship tech career: strong late-game pay, programming-gated promotions, and computer literacy as the foundation. It expects you to invest time and tuition before the job feels “easy.”

Basic computer — entry literacy; trained by the first software course wave. Programming — the real ladder stat; university-tier education pushes it higher. tip Start software development (apprenticeship) as soon as age and money allow. The university programming course requires that first program—skipping it blocks the entire senior path.

Unlike bartending or waitressing, developer ranks assume sequential courses: Apprenticeship-style software engineering track (computer skill, many in-game days). College-category advanced software / programming track chained after the first completion. Treat tuition as startup capital: a few months of teen work funds the first course if you budget.
Tech hiring uses a dedicated interview pool—expect logic, ethics, and stress questions. Intelligence helps learning speed globally, so academic characters promote faster with fewer calendar days.

Run school courses or digital marketing (computer-adjacent) if you need a cheaper bridge before formal dev tuition. Avoid burning out: low energy tanks interview performance indirectly through missed days. Pair with banker only if you love spreadsheets—both want calendar time. tip If your goal is maximum income per year played, developer is a marathon: commit or pick delivery or banker for a shorter ramp.

In Life Simulator Reloaded, work is how you earn steady money, train skills, and unlock quests. Most jobs require you to be not imprisoned, pass age gates, and meet skill or course thresholds as you climb ranks.

When a job is available, you apply and may face an interview: scripted questions where your answers and stats can affect the outcome. Some roles (for example teen part-time work) reuse a compact set of teen interview prompts; specialized careers use longer, role-specific question pools.

Each job defines levels (titles) with payment, skills learned per day, and requirements (skills, stats, or completed courses). A promotion ratio rolls over time—keep working, stay qualified, and you can move up. Higher ranks usually pay more but demand stronger skills. tip Before chasing a promotion, open the job’s level list and note hard gates (for example a course requirement or a skill floor). Finish the course or grind the skill before you stall for many in-game days.

Prefer answers that match the job theme (safety for acrobat, responsibility for teen jobs, composure for service roles). Communication, calmness, and sports help across many interviews; invest early if you job-hop often. If you fail an interview, improve skills and try again—there is no shame in treating it like a skill check.

Path Focus School jobs Part-time work while young Beggar Street survival and reputation Bartender Bar service, mixology, tips Cook Restaurant kitchen ladder Waitress Front-of-house service, tips Developer Tech track, education-heavy Banker Finance, economics progression Delivery driver Driving-based logistics Acrobat Performance and risky decisions Actor Fame-focused celebrity career Prison jobs Laundry and barber behind bars tip Pick one main career per life chapter (school vs. street vs. white-collar). Splitting attention spreads skill gains and slows promotions; specialization pays off faster.

When you are in prison, conventional careers pause. Two institutional jobs remain: laundry and barber (hairdressing). Both train practical skills, pay modest wages, and help you survive incarceration with something to do each day.

Role fantasy: washing, folding, keeping linens moving. Skill: cleaning rises quickly from daily passes (variable gains). Levels: amateur and regular washer tiers; higher tier expects strong cleaning already. tip If you expect a long sentence, laundry is the fastest way to rocket cleaning for post-release jobs like kitchen dish pit—think of it as involuntary training.

Role fantasy: cutting hair inside the yard or shop. Skill: haircutting (barber skill) is the focus; master tier also expects cleaning because hygiene rules the workshop. Levels: apprentice, normal, and master—each step raises pay slightly. Barber promotions need haircutting thresholds (50 for normal, 100 for master) plus cleaning for the final jump.
Neither prison job uses interview flows—you are assigned work by circumstance, not HR.

Pick laundry if you want one stat mastered fast; pick barber if you want a craft that pays marginally better at the top. Plan post-prison employment: haircutting supports civilian barber fantasies; cleaning supports cook or service roles. Stay out of fights when possible; injuries waste days you could spend grinding these skills. tip Treat prison jobs as stat bootcamps, not wealth engines. Your real payday returns when you walk free with a maxed utility skill.

School jobs are early-career roles aimed at ages roughly 16–22: low base pay, quick interviews, and steady skill drip while you study or explore the city. They are ideal for first money, sports or communication training, and learning the promotion loop without harsh gates.

Job What you do Skills emphasized Babysitter Watch neighborhood kids Calmness, communication Dog walker Walk pets Sports Tutor Help younger students Academics, communication Lawn mower Yard work Sports Newspaper delivery Route delivery Sports Grocery bagger Checkout support Communication Each job has beginner and experienced tiers. Experienced levels ask for higher skills (for example sports or communication thresholds) but pay a few units more per day. tip Tutor is the odd one out: it expects academics early. If you skipped school stats, start with dog walker, lawn mower, or bagger to fund courses or raise communication first.

Payments are small compared to mid-game careers—think of them as allowance plus training. Some roles can still trigger occasional tips or morale events, which helps a broke teen recover from bad days.

Line up one school job while you complete school courses or raise academics if you plan a knowledge-heavy life. Use interviews to learn the question patterns; failures are cheap at this stage. Resign cleanly when you outgrow the pay band—bank skills, not nostalgia. tip If you want sports for later acrobat, delivery, or combat-adjacent content, dog walker + newspaper delivery stack sports gains efficiently while paying you something back.

Waitresses run the restaurant floor: communication-heavy shifts, table service statistics, and a tip tracker separate from base wages. The job pairs naturally with customer service training and social stat growth.

Communication — primary requirement for promotions and many random events. Cleaning shows up at trainee levels because spills and resets are part of the shift. tip Grab the customer service course while you are still a trainee. It is tailored to this ladder and softens both promotions and angry-customer events.
Expect questions about allergies, mixed-up orders, rush hour, and manager feedback. Decisions sometimes pit etiquette against speed—higher communication makes the “smooth” branches reliable.

Milestones usually include: Serve 50 tables — accumulates as you work the floor. Promote to senior waitress — proves you cleared the mid-rank skill checks. Earn 200 in tips — tracked across your waitress career, not a single shift. Cash plus bragging rights reward players who commit to service.

Keep morale healthy; rude customers are scripted to drain it. If you chase the quest, prioritize tip events when your communication can carry the skill check. Transition to bartender or cook later if you want the same location with different skills. tip Looks helps many social careers indirectly by easing requirement math—if promotions stall despite high communication, check whether stat gates are hiding on the next level.
The airport is a city travel hub. Today it centers on sightseeing flights rather than a full world-map travel sim — think of it as premium morale + stat tourism with a weekly cadence.

Sightseeing flight — Adult-only. Pay for coastal, mountain, or city routes (increasing price). Each route refunds different morale, calmness or communication, and stat bumps (looks or intelligence depending on route). Energy cost is baked into the trip. Weekly cooldown between flights. Small chance for a souvenir item on completion.

When you are flush with cash and need a big morale reset plus a permanent stat nudge. Less efficient than grinding skills, but fast and flavorful. Strategy If you only afford one flight in a week, compare route stat rewards to your current build (e.g., mountain/city skew int, coastal skews looks + calmness).
The souvenir drop is the main extra proc; broader intercontinental travel mechanics may expand in future updates — the airport UI is the natural hook.
The bank is the finance spot in the city: gold trading lives here, and the banker job path is tied to this building.

Buy gold — While not in prison, spend cash at the current gold price. Choose how many coins to buy; large holdings count toward gold hoarder achievements at 10, 100, and 1,000 coins. Sell gold — Cash out coins at slightly below the buy price for quick money. Work as a banker — Interview-heavy career with rising titles; see Jobs: Banker.

When you want to hold wealth in gold during shaky economy moments, or chase achievements for stockpiling bullion. Selling after a price jump can pay off if you watch the market. Strategy Compare the listed buy and sell prices before flipping — the spread means you lose a little per coin versus the mid price, so quick trades only make sense on big moves.
Random economy or identity stories may mention banking, but buying and selling are up to you. Prices move with the wider economy, not with room chatter.
The bar is a city nightlife spot. It mixes money sinks, mini-games / decisions, and social payoffs — and it supports bartender work (see Jobs: Bartender).

Pub quiz — Pays an entry fee, then a decision check; success returns cash, intelligence, communication, morale, and tracks quiz wins toward an achievement. Can meet a new NPC sometimes. Karaoke — Costs a small cover; click-game performance. Success boosts communication and morale, can add a friend, and awards a karaoke achievement. Arm wrestling — Decision challenge vs. a patron; wins stack toward arm wrestling achievements.

Spend disposable cash when you want int + communication together (quiz), or morale spikes (karaoke). Good stop while pursuing celebrity / social arcs that care about friends met in the wild. Strategy Space quiz attempts — it has a multi-day cooldown so you cannot spam it daily for infinite prizes.
Bar outcomes sometimes inject random NPCs into your relationship list after strong performances. Bartender shifts (job) add separate on-the-clock events not tied to patron actions.
The black market is in the slum district, not the polished downtown loop. Everything here is crime-focused: high rewards, witness risk, and possible prison fallout.

Smuggle goods — Choose a size of run (small crate up to luxury). A reaction mini-game; you can skip with gems for a price tied to the payout. Success: large cash, criminal and evil skill gains; witnesses may still add wanted days. Failure: crime pressure plus you may face a police chase — lose that and you can land in prison. You can only smuggle again after a monthly cooldown. Forge documents — Pay 500, confirm you accept the crime, then pass a risk check to get a fake ID (and a related achievement). Failure costs the attempt and adds crime pressure.

Only when your run can survive 25–40+ day wanted spikes or a prison detour. A burner phone lowers witness odds when smuggling succeeds. Strategy If you are already wanted, the game skips the “are you sure?” step — faster flow, same risk.
Witness and road escape moments layer on top of smuggling. See Crime: Committing crimes for how heat works.
The cemetery is a quiet city location built around a single powerful daily action: prayer. Outcomes are randomized but always interact with calmness, and often morale or stats.

Pray — Once per game day. Costs a little energy, trains calmness, and rolls among outcomes: peaceful morale boost, deep reflection (+ intelligence), finding coins on a grave, eerie wind (mixed morale but big calmness/honor), or ghostly whispers (scary: morale/health hit but huge calmness growth). Repeated visits count toward a cemetery devotee achievement.

Best on low-morale days when you can accept variance, or when training calmness for decisions and stress events. Avoid if you are already injured and cannot risk the rare health penalty branch. Strategy Treat prayer as a calmness engine first; the coin branch is a nice bonus, not the main reason to go.
The prayer roll is the event bundle — no separate hidden queue. Some items (for example holy water hooks in content) can interact with cemetery logic in other systems; watch logs when experimenting.
The electronics shop sells phones, computers, and related gear via the market UI, and offers a repair gig that pays scaled cash.

Repair gadgets — Cooldown-gated. Burns energy, then runs a decision check. Success: random payout, basic computer + programming skill, statistic toward gadget achievements, rare bonus component money roll. Failure: morale hit but minor skill consolation.

Early money for teens who lack jobs, or mid-game skill bridging before developer interviews. Buy electronics here when you need internet-gated actions elsewhere. Strategy Stack repairs after sleep / energy recovery — the flat energy penalty hurts on an already tired character.
Rare bonus payout log after success; otherwise interactions are self-contained. See Items: Electronics for what to buy.
The gun shop sells weapons and ammunition through the item market while you are at this location, and hosts a shooting lane mini-game.

Target practice — Costs money and energy on a cooldown. Stop-the-bar timing mini-game: success trains fighting and calmness, boosts morale. Owning a rifle widens the hit window slightly. Tight-window success can award sharpshooter achievements. Browse firearms — Purchase weapons for other systems (crime, hunting modules) when unlocked in the catalog.

If you plan combat-heavy arcs, train fighting here alongside Gym boxing — different skill mix (adds calmness). Buy hardware before jobs or quests that check gear. Strategy Practice before you need fighting checks; failed runs still teach a little fighting but waste cash and mood.
No bespoke random queue; achievement thresholds (sharpshooter) and inventory checks (rifle bonus) are the hidden depth.
The city gym is the main paid training spot for sports, looks, and fighting — separate from the prison gym while you are jailed.

Workout / lift weights — Costs money each session; skill challenge reps. Success trains sports, raises looks, and spends energy through the activity. Available here or at the prison gym if you are inside. Boxing match — Entry fee plus a timing mini-game (stop the marker in the green zone). Win: cash, fighting and sports, morale, and wins count toward knockout-style achievements. Lose: big health and morale loss. Boxing gloves make the timing window a bit wider.

Prioritize when you are building fighting for crime, patrol fights, or brawls, or looks for careers and romance. Skip if you are broke — losing a boxing match hurts. Strategy Wear boxing gloves before matches; the extra window combines with your fighting and sports levels for easier timing.
No location-only story beyond achievement milestones and combat stat growth; prison has its own gym beats in Prison life.
Home is tied to your current house. It is your default base for domestic actions, relaxing, and many childhood activities. You must actually have housing for the location to appear.

Cook fish — Turn raw fish into cooked fish at home (cooking skill); other meal prep may use items and recipes elsewhere. Garden — Once per day (when available): click-game tending, cooking and calmness skill, morale; periodic herb harvests and a related achievement. Watch television — Requires the TV furniture in use; pick a genre for morale (and sometimes intelligence on documentaries). Cooldown between uses. Early life — Babies and children get actions such as babble, tantrum, nap, play with toys, and similar home-adjacent routines.

Use home to recover through the day loop (advance days / rest via your normal play flow), save money by cooking caught fish instead of dining out, and stack calmness + cooking from gardening before stressful jobs or crime. Strategy Buy and use the TV furniture early if you want a cheap, repeatable morale (and occasional int) boost without leaving the house.
Beggar and other hooks sometimes care whether you are at home vs. out in the city, changing odds and logs. Throwing rocks (vandalism) is intentionally not available at home.
The hospital is the legitimate medical hub in the city. It focuses on disease workflow and optional cosmetic surgery — both cost money.

See a doctor — If you have active diseases, the doctor marks them as hospital-cared, which enables cure chances over time in the disease system. With nothing active, you get a “no disease” style outcome. Plastic surgery — Adult-only; exponential price each time you use it. Large looks stat bump on success.

As soon as you suspect sickness (symptoms / logs), visit once to register care — cures still tick with chance afterward, but doctor visit is the gate. Save plastic surgery for late-game money dumps when looks gates block promotions or fame. Strategy Compare with Witch house — potions can wipe diseases in one use, while hospital is the “system” path tied to ongoing cure rolls.
Disease cure ticks after care are handled in simulation, not as a single hospital button. Prison infirmary mirrors doctor access while locked up.
The jeweler handles high-end accessories. Shopping lists diamonds and display pieces, while the spotlight action is professional appraisal.

Appraise items — Requires carrying rings, coins, or similar flagged valuables and paying a fee on a weekly cadence. Decision flow: success grants intelligence and morale; owning fake rings risks exposure (looks + morale crash) or, on luck, selling the fake for big money. Gold coins add int even before the decision resolves.

After crime, treasure, or relationship gifts leave you unsure what you hold. Also useful before pawn-style choices elsewhere so you know real vs. fake. Strategy Never appraise fakes unless you accept failure risk — success can dump a worthless ring for 500 cash, failure tanks looks.
The appraisal decision bundles the drama; no roaming ghost events. Pair with Market and Black market for how goods enter inventory.
The public library is the civilian reading room. The same read a book option also appears at the prison library when you are locked up — same activity, different place.

Read a book — Choose any skill you still have room to improve; a challenge simulates turning pages. Success gives a large boost to that skill plus intelligence, clears the book you were working through, and costs energy. Failure still teaches a little. Prisoners use the same flow to study behind bars.

Best when you want one skill to climb off the clock — languages, niche job skills, or shoring up weak spots before choices and job interviews. Strategy Each skill remembers how far you are into a book until you finish — start a session when you have energy so you are not stuck mid-book when you are drained.
Nothing unique to the room beyond reading-related achievements elsewhere in the game. For jail reading, see Prison life.
The market is the general commerce floor. Expect category shopping (food, gear, and more depending on modules) plus a standout social action.

Shop the stalls — Use the standard buy/sell flows while standing here; stock rotates with game economy rules and unlocks. Haggle — Once per day when allowed. Decision-based persuasion check. Success: free food or misc item, better table if persuasion is high. Failure: morale hit and a temporary ban from haggling (tracked in storage) — do not spam carelessly.

Your default pit stop whenever you need consumables or to liquidate loot. Add haggle on days you want free inventory padding and persuasion training. Strategy If haggling bans you after a bad roll, wait out the cooldown — the game stores a “banned until day” flag.
Black market and specialist shops split illegal or luxury stock; market remains the bread-and-butter storefront. Random city events may mention shopping but rarely replace the core UI.

In Life Simulator Reloaded, locations are places your character can travel to. Each spot unlocks different actions (things you can do that turn), jobs (when you are employed there), shopping categories, and random events that fire when you visit or pass time.

City and public areas — Most of the game happens here: home, parks, shops, school, and services. You can move freely between them unless an action or story state blocks you (for example, prison). Prison — When you are imprisoned, the city list is replaced by jail locations (yard, dormitory, prison gym, library, infirmary, cafeteria, chapel, workshop, and solitary). Routine, jobs, and fights are covered in Crime & Prison: Prison life. Strategy Keep a mental “shopping route”: Market for general goods and haggling, specialist shops for weapons, electronics, and jewelry, and Black Market only when you accept crime risk.

Location Role Home Housing hub: cook, garden, TV (with furniture), childhood activities Park Outdoors: jog, busk, flowers, playground; fishing ties to events Bar Social: pub quiz, karaoke, arm wrestling Restaurant Meals, cooking challenge mini-game Gym Paid workout, boxing match mini-game Hospital Diagnose diseases, plastic surgery Police station Surrender when wanted, volunteer patrol Cemetery Pray once per day; varied outcomes Airport Sightseeing flights (morale, stats, souvenir chance) Public library Read books to train a chosen skill + intelligence Market Haggle for free loot; general buying/selling UI Gun shop Target practice mini-game (fighting skill) Electronics shop Repair gadgets for cash (decision + skills) Jewelry store Appraise rings and valuables Black market Smuggling mini-game, forge documents (crime) Bank Buy/sell gold (trading), banker career City school Study, skip class, cafeteria, talk to teacher Witch house Special shop items (potions, life stone); arrival flavor
Hunter's Guild and Dark Forest appear when the Monster Hunter content is in play. See Modules: Monster Hunter.
