The park is an outdoor city location focused on health, sports, social skills, and light money opportunities.

Collect flowers — Nature gather action while you are at the park (ages 4+). Playground — Young children play here for morale, sports skill, and tutorial quest progress. Jog — Daily click-game: energy cost, health and looks upside, sports skill; chance to find a wallet (return for honor/morale or keep for cash + evil skill). Binoculars improve find odds. Long-term jogs unlock a jogger achievement. Busking / street performance — Decision-based tips; can meet NPCs and rarely a talent scout bonus payout.

Train sports and looks cheaply, farm honor (return wallet) or evil (keep wallet), and grind communication + cash early as a teen/adult. Strategy Bring binoculars before jogging if you want more wallet events; decide in advance whether you are roleplaying honor or greed for the choice branch.

Fishing is often triggered as a friend invite question (not a single permanent “Fish” button): success can yield raw fish, fishing skill, and rare money bag luck. Random trackers can fire park-related prompts while you live your week.
The police station is where lawful and wanted stories collide: you can turn yourself in or help the force for pay and honor.

Surrender — Visible while wanted. Cuts remaining sentence roughly in half (minimum one day) and sends you straight to prison. Use when heat is unbearable or you want to rip the bandage off. Volunteer patrol — Not wanted, not imprisoned. Decision-based night patrol: energy cost, honor + communication on success, cash stipend. Can spawn a sub-decision to confront a crook for bonus money or take a health hit if it goes wrong. Repeatable on a cooldown; many clears unlock vigilante-style achievements.

Surrender before random arrests screw a fragile run if you accept jail. Patrol is a mid-game honor + money grind when you are clean and can spare energy. Strategy Patrol’s optional fight branch is a skill check — raise fighting at the Gym if you hate losing health to failed interventions.
Crime module pickpocket / GTA / smuggling outcomes elsewhere can eventually force you here via wanted state; patrol is the main benign random chain at the building itself.
The restaurant is where you eat out for instant needs and play a cooking challenge. It is also the workplace for waitress and cook paths (see Jobs).

Dine out — Pick a meal tier (street food up to chef's table) if you can afford it; restores health, energy, and morale once per day. The top tier can raise intelligence. Small chance to meet a stranger (counts toward social achievements). Cooking challenge — Weekly; skill challenge with cooking rewards, cash on success, and a chance at a chef's knife if your cooking is high enough. Failure costs morale and energy.

Use cheap tiers when you are hurt or exhausted; use gourmet or chef's table before exams or checks that care about intelligence. Run the challenge when you want money and cooking together. Strategy If you want the knife, raise cooking first — the bonus item only rolls after a successful challenge, and your cooking level matters.
Dates and anniversaries can pick the restaurant when it fits, which changes flavor and cost. If you work here, job events stack on top of what you do as a customer.
School is the daytime education hub for teens and adults. It combines free actions with the Education screen for paid courses and degrees.

Study — Daily challenge: big gains to academics and intelligence on success, partial reward on failure, costs energy. Skip class — Morale buff with an academics penalty; you may get caught (worse for academics). Cafeteria hangout — Once per day morale and communication. Talk to teacher — Academics and communication; sometimes extra mentorship for more academics. Enroll in courses — Use Education while you are here to buy lessons that finish over days (see Education).

Every day during student arcs to keep academics high before exams and job options. Combine cafeteria and teacher when you want social growth without going to the Bar. Strategy Skipping is tempting for morale — keep academics high enough if you rely on scholarships or school-related story beats.
While enrolled, random scenes can play out here — cafeteria drama, bullies, and similar moments — separate from the main action buttons. Keep showing up to see them.
The witch house lives in the woods area — a secluded alternative medicine vendor with gem and cash priced curios.

Shop exclusive stock — While physically here (or in special cases such as after death for select items), buy potions that clear all active diseases on use, life stones that can revive you once on death (long buy cooldown after purchase), and other witch-tagged gear listed in the market sheet. Arrive — The location emits a door / witch flavor log the first time you step in to sell the fantasy tone.

Emergency disease wipes if you cannot wait for Hospital cure ticks, or hardcore insurance via life stone before dangerous crime/monster content. Strategy Potions are pricey — compare 1000 cash / 15 gems style costs against a hospital visit if you only need diagnosis + patience.

Life stone hooks run on death (consuming the item). Few overworld traps fire just from standing in the hut — drama is mostly inventory based. Compare timing and cost with Hospital disease care when planning builds.

Life Simulator Reloaded runs on situations that fire as you play: where you are, what you own, your job, and optional story packs all feed into what can happen next. What feels “random” is usually weighted chance plus hidden prerequisites (skills, story progress, how far along a relationship is).

Common moments when something new can happen: Day pass — start or end of a simulated day; good for weather, news, maintenance, and ambient life. Location change — arriving somewhere can spawn encounters (school, street, workplace). After specific actions — finishing a job shift, using an item, or resolving a choice. Story packs — crime, celebrity, and monster content add their own encounters on top of everyday life. Events can show as logs with popups, choice dialogs, or quiet changes to your stats—always read the text before tapping through. tip If an event “never happens,” you are usually missing a location, minimum stat, or story step. Progress the main loop a few days elsewhere, then return.

Day-pass events simulate life noise: small wins, small losses, social pings, illness teases, opportunity knocks. They keep long runs from feeling sterile. Handling them: Stable meters first — low health, energy, or morale skew outcomes toward harsher branches. Save gems for branches that threaten jail time, major stat loss, or quest failure if you play hardcore. Note recurring patterns — some chains repeat daily until you complete a milestone.
School content clusters around education, social growth, and early career seeds. Expect truancy vs. study tradeoffs, bully or friend arcs, and skills that pay off much later in your character’s life.

While in prison, events lean on relationships inside jail, prison reputation, and fights. Outcomes can reduce sentence, start brawls, or offer risky choices. Read risk carefully: a short temper can extend your stay.

Monster storyline content adds combat-style and exploration encounters—often tied to specific places, gear (trackers, weapons), or quest stages. Preparation beats rushing in blind: gear, skills, and escape options matter.

Situation Approach Unclear risk Choose the option that protects meters first, money second. Skill check shown Train the skill or use a boost or gem if the prize is unique. Repeat failure Change location, job, or relationship context—events often key off where you are in life. tip Some story branches block each other: if something feels “locked out,” you may have already gone down a path that rules out the other outcome earlier in the run. Exact event lists evolve with updates; this page describes behavior, not a fixed loot table.
Gems are the premium currency in Life Simulator Reloaded. They are rarer than cash and are meant for clutch saves, skips, and exclusive purchases—not for bypassing every minor inconvenience.

Typical spends include: Spend Why use it Decision boosts Tip high-stakes choices in your favor (legal trouble, romance locks, career gambits). You can still fail, but the odds improve. Mini-game skips Instantly pass timed challenges when you are about to lose a reward or take a penalty. Market (gem-priced items) Gear, cosmetics, or utility items sold for gems instead of cash. Prison lawyer 15 gems — hire representation for a large sentence reduction (a chunk of your remaining time, with a minimum cut); the game may limit how often this applies in a given situation. Guard bribe 5 gems — some prison interactions expect a small gem payment (repeatable where the game allows). tip Think in days saved and unique rewards: if a boost prevents a week of jail or saves a one-time reward, gems are well spent.

Boosts improve your chance of success on a choice—you can still fail; use when the upside is huge and you are close to passing. Skips remove having to play the challenge—best when the mini-game is new to you or timing would ruin a fair attempt. See Mini-games for per-game tactics so you need fewer skips over time.

Lawyer (15 gems) when you have many prison days left—a long sentence means a bigger slice of time saved. Skips on first-time quest steps that gate story packs or trophies you cannot easily redo. Boosts on all-or-nothing decisions where failure wipes stats or relationships. Gem market items only for things that unlock actions or lasting convenience; skip pure flavor unless you enjoy the flex. Avoid gem-spending loops on problems you can solve with cash and time—usually better to work another in-game week. tip Hoard a small emergency stack (e.g. 10–20 gems) if you play ironman-style; one bad encounter should not end a long run for lack of a few gems.

Income sources vary by how you play and by store offers (in-app purchases, rewards, events). Treat gems as budgeted, not infinite—the toughest spends assume you sometimes pay real money or accumulate slowly, so spend deliberately. Costs can change in updates—always check the in-game confirm dialog before you spend.

Mini-games are timed challenges wrapped in story. The screen shows title, reward hints, and a gem skip; your job is to meet the success condition before you fail. Difficulty often scales with context (crime vs. school), so the same kind of challenge can feel faster or stricter in different scenes. tip Mute distractions and tap once per decision—double taps ruin lockpicking and cue-based games. If you are struggling, a gem skip beats repeating a harsh penalty loop.

Core: A marker moves along a line; tap to stop inside the green band. Strategy: Watch speed more than the band’s position—learn the rhythm for one pace, then adjust when the bar speeds up. Common for pickpocketing and precision timing moments.

Core: A rotating pick; tap when it aligns with the sweet spot on an arc. Strategy: Anticipate delay between what you see and when your tap registers; aim for the center of the window, not the edge. The theme is locks and car theft—expect tighter windows at higher stakes.
Core: A Simon-style grid—cells flash in order; repeat the sequence. Strategy: Chunk the pattern (pairs or edges-first); say the order quietly. Used for alarm codes and prison escape style setups.

Core: Direction arrows show briefly, then hide; reproduce them with the arrow pad. Strategy: Turn arrows into body motion (up = ceiling) immediately—abstract memorization fades fast. Used for fight combos and ordered quick-time scenes.

Core: Green cue = tap on time; red cue = do not tap (each has its own timer). Strategy: This mixes holding back and reacting fast—slow your first impulse on mixed rounds. Used for street crossing, “don’t move” beats, and discipline checks.

Core: Rapid taps fill a meter that drops over time; beat the time limit. Strategy: Use two thumbs if comfortable; short bursts beat uneven spam when the meter falls quickly. Used for forcing doors, struggling free, and sprinting beats.

Core: A marker drifts; use left/right to stay inside the center zone until the timer clears. Strategy: Small corrections—big moves overshoot. Used for meditation, balance, and stress needle style scenes.

Core: Targets appear in random spots; tap each before it vanishes; hit the target count under a global timer. Strategy: Scan with peripheral vision; hit soonest-to-expire targets first. Used for riot reflex scenes and whack-a-mole style challenges.

Core: Memorize the grid, then find the one cell with a different icon. Strategy: Take a row-by-row mental picture on the memorization pass; on the hidden phase, eliminate identical neighbors first. Used for inspection and detail puzzles.

Core: Flip two cards to match pairs; wrong flips use up your try budget; a countdown adds pressure. Strategy: Open four corners early to map symbols; remember pair locations, not single tiles. Used for concentration and safe-cracking style puzzles. Skills: Some actions are easier if you have trained the right skills—if a challenge feels smoother after leveling up, that is intentional. Difficulty and timing can change in updates; use in-game feedback as the final word.

Cash flow is the backbone of a stable life: rent, gear, education, and emergencies all pull from the same wallet. Life Simulator Reloaded ties income to jobs, stores wealth in property, and lets you trade through the market—while gems sit alongside as premium currency (see Gems & boosts).

Primary income: Working shifts, promotions, and job-specific bonuses. Skill gates: Better jobs need skills; skills need time and sometimes courses (often a money sink upfront, payoff later). Promotions: Looks makes promotion skill checks a bit easier, so investing in appearance can help you climb pay tiers faster. tip Line up one career track early: bouncing between unrelated entry jobs burns days. Pick a path whose skills stack (e.g. service, tech, crime-adjacent) for compounding raises.

Housing and related systems let you: Pay rent or invest in better living (comfort often feeds energy and morale indirectly through the actions available at home). Use furniture and home activities where the game offers them—some pieces give daily bonuses or extra options tied to being at home. Property is both a status symbol and a stability tool: a safer home rhythm makes it easier to hold a job and recover your meters.

The market lists items with cash prices; some entries also offer a gem price. You can: Buy consumables, gear, gifts, and progression items. Sell surplus loot when the game lets you—clearing inventory turns clutter into runway. Watch for extra stock unlocked by optional story packs: crime, celebrity, and monster content can add niche goods. tip Before big purchases, ask: Does this unlock actions, save meters, or speed a quest? Decorative buys are fine for flavor; progression buys win tight runs.
Gems are not regular cash. They buy skips, boosts, and select market exclusives. Budget them for moments where failure costs days or stats—not for every small inconvenience. Details: Gems & boosts.

Promote on schedule — meet skill checks before burning time on side hustles. Stack passive-friendly days — work → recover → repeat beats constant risky grinds. Sell what you do not need after events that flood inventory. Invest in education when a course unlocks a higher wage tier; treat tuition as ROI, not sunk cost. Balance and prices can change; always confirm numbers in the live build.

People are systems: they gate actions, trigger events, and change how risky choices play out. Life Simulator Reloaded groups NPC ties into categories, then tracks how strong and how positive each bond is.

Category Role FAMILY Parents, siblings, relatives—baseline support network and story hooks. LOVE Romantic partners; marriage-style titles and intimate interactions. FRIENDS Social circle outside work; parties, favors, emotional backup. CO_WORKER Colleagues; can shift toward friendship through shared actions. JAIL Inmates and prison-specific NPCs when you are serving time (crime module). Categories decide which actions appear and which events can fire—not every NPC can be handled the same way.

Bonds are not binary. Alongside category, you will see relationship flavor such as: Love — romantic depth; often paired with the LOVE category. Friendship — trust and warmth; common in FRIENDS and can grow from CO_WORKER. Hate — hostility; unlocks confrontations, sabotage, or avoidance paths. Moving someone from neutral to friend (or rival) usually takes repeated interactions: gifts, shared activities, supporting them in decisions, or choosing dialogue-aligned actions when offered. tip Coworkers → friends: The game can promote a colleague into the FRIENDS category after enough positive social actions—useful for both morale and job events.

Invest time and appropriate actions (dates, gifts, supportive choices). Watch for blocking statuses (e.g. existing partner rules); some paths require clearing or accepting consequences. LOVE category NPCs often tie into family planning and long-term story beats—pace your career stress so you can afford the social maintenance.

Family members anchor early game tutorials and mid-game obligations (events, money asks, emotional swings). Keeping morale and money buffers helps you say “yes” to family moments without tanking your meters.

Behind bars, JAIL NPCs mesh with prison reputation and fight/interaction systems. Allies can open safer choices; enemies increase tension. Treat prison as its own social graph—your yard cred matters as much as your cell routine.

Interact regularly — neglected NPCs drift or trigger negative events. Match gifts and actions to what the character cares about (job, hobbies, story flags). Avoid stacking betrayals — hate status is harder to unwind than friendship is to build. Recover your own meters first; a depleted character picks worse social options. tip If a relationship menu feels quiet, change location or advance the day—many social hooks are tied to place and calendar, not a single screen. NPC names and scenes vary by module; categories and rules stay consistent.

Your character’s numbers drive survival, careers, and special storylines. Life Simulator Reloaded separates status meters (what you feel today) from core stats (long-term potential) and dynamic stats (context-specific reputation).

Meter Range What it means Health 0 up to your maximum (you start at 100; some upgrades raise that cap) Physical condition. Energy 0 up to your maximum Stamina for actions and the day. Morale 0 up to your maximum Mental well-being and motivation. Death: If any of these three hits 0, your character is considered dead—not only health. Danger zone: When any meter is 20 or below, you are in danger (warnings and risky outcomes can follow). Stay above that line when you can. Restore meters with rest, food, safe activities, and items or events that explicitly refill them. Pushing every day without recovery is how runs spiral. tip Treat 20 as your “red line” for health, energy, and morale. Heal and rest before you scrape the floor.

Stat Range What it does Intelligence 1–200 Higher intelligence helps you learn skills faster, so jobs and training pay off sooner over a long career. Looks 1–200 Higher looks eases promotion checks—employers judge you a bit more favorably on skill requirements, so social investment can open higher pay tiers. New characters start with both stats in a starter band; training, education, life choices, and items can move them over time. Upgrades that raise your maximum health, energy, or morale give you more room to work with during hard chapters (crime, fame grind, illness, and similar). tip High intelligence compounds over a long career; high looks softens promotion walls. Plan early if you want a specialist build vs. a social-climber build.

Some story paths add dynamic stats (they use the same kind of scale as your other stats while they matter), for example: Prison reputation — how inmates see you; affects intimidation, fights, and opportunities behind bars. Fame — celebrity visibility; amplifies outcomes in star-related content (films, events, public life). These often rise from actions tied to that storyline (fights, performances, quests). They are not always visible from day one; they show up when the relevant content is in play.

Goal Typical levers Health / energy / morale Sleep, eat, low-risk routines, medical or wellness actions, story rewards. Intelligence School, reading, courses, brainy jobs and decisions. Looks Grooming, fitness, fashion, social and beauty-adjacent actions. Prison rep Dominance, winning fights, prison social actions (crime storyline). Fame Celebrity career path, media and public events (celebrity storyline). Mechanics may receive balance updates; when in doubt, check in-game tooltips and patch notes.
The celebrity pack adds a fame path: public attention, star-making jobs, and story beats that treat your character as a public figure instead of an anonymous citizen.

Fame tracks how widely you are known. Higher fame: Unlocks premium jobs, especially acting and performance-related careers Ties into quests and achievements around spotlight moments Changes social reactions — people recognize you more often tip Fame works best alongside looks and performance skills you can train in the base game — casting and big breaks often check several stats, not fame alone.

The pack supports actor / entertainer style careers: Audition-style steps and promotions through the job system Story choices and events around press, scandals, and big breaks Money can spike when you hit it big, but downside events also show up (public shame, stalker-style beats, and similar) info Treat fame as a meter that unlocks doors — exact job names and promotion steps appear in-game as you play.

Unlock the celebrity pack and take a job that puts you in the public eye. Train relevant skills (performance, speech, looks where the game asks for them). Engage with pack events — repeated positive beats usually raise fame faster than waiting. Reinvest income in education or grooming if something blocks the next tier. aviso Fame without savings is risky. Bad press can hit morale or money; early on, keep a normal job in mind as a backup.

The core package is the default game: every player has it. It defines the ordinary life arc — school, jobs, housing, romance, aging, economy, diseases, travel, and the bulk of quests unrelated to crime, fame, or monsters.

Pillar Examples Careers Service jobs, office paths, trades, education gating Locations Home, city services, shops, school, hospital, witch house, etc. Stats Intelligence, looks, and the shared skill / need systems Social Family, love, friends, coworkers — see Social interactions Health Health / energy / morale, diseases, hospital treatment Economy Money, market, rent, furniture info Think of core as the simulation chassis. Optional modules bolt crime, celebrity, and monster arcs onto the same character sheet.

Even with every DLC active, you still: Pay rent, work jobs, and manage needs Use hospital (or witch) for disease — prison clinic reuses doctor action when jailed Progress generic achievements and tutorials tip Strong core fundamentals (stable job, health buffer, savings) make crime or hunting side paths less run-ending when they punish you.

documents.t: The crime pack turns Life Simulator Reloaded into a crime drama when you want it: steal, smuggle, forge, run from police, and — if caught — play a whole second phase inside prison.

System What you’ll notice Crime actions Pickpocketing, vehicle theft, smuggling, forgery, and more Wanted A timer that stacks; police can interrupt you when you travel Prison Its own area, locations, a daily prison-life skill, and random events Prison reputation A stat that matters mainly while you are sentenced Fights Prison-only combat against other prisoners Items Contraband, improvised weapons, blueprints, luxury prison loot aviso Going to prison usually forces you to quit normal jobs and can remove prison-tagged items when you get out. Plan for that reset.

Mini-games: memory challenges, timing and focus trials, crafting and smuggling sequences, training mash-style tasks, riot-style target rounds, plus more tied to random events (parole hearings, shakedowns, and similar beats). Interactions: greet, intimidate, trade, share meals, gossip, ask for protection, fight, defend a friend, steal, extort, recruit for a gang, bribe a guard. Quests: long arcs like Survivor, Scholar, and Kingpin — see Prison quests guide.
Crime overview Prison life — full mechanic tables Prison fights — moves and opponent difficulty

The Monster Hunter pack adds hunts in the dark forest and related areas: buy a zombie tracker, get daily detection rolls while you carry it, fight different monster types, loot materials for crafting, and upgrade the tracker through five levels.

Unlock the pack and travel to guild-related locations (see your in-game map). Buy a Zombie Tracker — it enables daily detection while you have it on you. When something is detected, use hunt actions with gear like a rifle, silver dagger, or holy water. Spend drops (zombie eyes, bone fragments, essences, and similar) to level the tracker — higher levels let stronger and rarer monsters appear. tip Upgrades use different material mixes at different levels; farm what you need for the next step so you can reach level 5 for the full monster pool, including demons.

Type What to expect Zombie Common to very rare tiers; early ones are easier, late ones are much tougher Skeleton Bone loot; middling difficulty Witch Essence- and powder-style drops; magic-themed attacks Demon Shows up with a high-level tracker; among the hardest fights Exact toughness and rewards scale with rarity in-game — you’ll see it when you fight.
Each day, the tracker can roll whether a monster appears and which kinds your current level allows. Higher tracker level means riskier encounters but often better loot.
You get options like rifle shots, silver dagger strikes, throwable holy water, and enemy patterns such as bites, punches, and spit that get nastier on tougher foes.

There are kill count goals (for example milestones at 1, 10, 100, and 200 zombies), first epic / first legendary style feats, and rewards for a maxed tracker. Quests tie into buying the tracker, first kills, and crafting beats. aviso Hunting costs health and ammo. Stock food and know how to reach care before long forest grinds — illnesses from the base health system still apply.

Life Simulator Reloaded includes a core experience plus three optional content packs. Each pack adds locations, jobs, items, quests, and mechanics into the same world. You buy or unlock them in the modules store, and they become part of your save.

Module What it adds Core Base city, careers, education, health, relationships, housing — the full default game Crime Illegal actions, wanted level and prison, life inside jail, prison fights and special items Celebrity Fame-driven careers, acting and spotlight-style content Monster Hunter Hunter’s guild, dark forest hunting, tracker gear, monster fights and crafting info Only core is always available. Crime, Celebrity, and Monster Hunter are optional. If a guide mentions prison or monsters, that content needs the matching pack.

Together, the packs define: City and travel — where you can go and how places connect Actions — what you can do at each location Shops and schools — what you can buy or study Quests and achievements — extra goals and rewards tip Pick packs that match how you want to play: Crime for outlaw runs, Celebrity for fame and performance careers, Monster Hunter for hunting and combat-loot loops. You can use several in one long life.
Core — baseline sim pillars Crime — illegal play and prison Celebrity — fame path Monster Hunter — hunting flow
Optional lifestyle and exploration arcs with varied milestones. Several begin in young adulthood (ages 18–23).

Starts: Around age 4. Must complete before age 10. Milestones (4): Play on the playground. Take a nap. Play with toys. Meditate. Reward: $50 and a teddy bear. Completing the quest also unlocks the Childhood Champion achievement. Difficulty: Easy — plan a few child-years ahead so you do not age out.
Four milestones — mix of selfie, arm wrestle, deep conversation, and sports with other people (see in-game text). Difficulty: Medium — needs NPCs or friends available for each interaction type.
Five milestones: haunted house, marathon, escape room, cave, bungee jump. Difficulty: Medium–hard (some activities are rare or stat-gated).

Five milestones: ethical choices such as rejecting a bribe, helping an accident victim, refusing stolen goods, reporting cheating, returning a found phone. Difficulty: Medium — watch for decision popups in the world.
Four milestones: sports sessions, marathon, gym with someone (5×), blood donation. Difficulty: Medium.
Four milestones: finish 3 courses, study together 10×, teach skills 5×, join a book club. Difficulty: Medium — pairs well with education and social systems.
Five milestones: shelter volunteering, petition, blood donation, help a lost tourist, rescue an animal. Difficulty: Medium.
Four milestones: Buy wedding outfit. Plan the wedding. Invite someone to the wedding. Get married. Difficulty: Medium — needs a relationship path advanced enough to marry.
These quests reward grinding a job or school path and mastering promotions.

Starts: Automatically when you take the beggar job. Milestone Requirement Street grind Beg 100 times (tracked on your character). Status Promote to Owner of the region (top beggar rank). Income Earn $500 total from begging (tracked separately from the 100 begs). Reward: $150 in current game data (some older notes may say $100). Tips: Work outside home so beg actions and day-pass ticks count. Train persuasion and survive in streets for promotions. Difficulty: Medium (time sink).
Serve 100 cocktails on the job. Reach Master bartender rank. Earn $300 in tips total. Tips: Stack shifts at the bar; higher skill and good decisions improve tips. Difficulty: Medium.
Serve 50 tables. Promote to Senior waitress. Earn $200 in tips. Tips: Similar to bartender — consistent work and successful service events. Difficulty: Medium.
Pass a school exam. Perform in a talent show or debate. Help a teacher (school interaction milestone). Difficulty: Easy–medium — stay enrolled and attend school events.
Starts: Around age 14. Land your first part-time job. Get promoted at that job. Tips: Check job board / available teen jobs early so the quest has time to finish. Difficulty: Easy.
Monster content lives in the Monster Hunter module. You need the zombie tracker and guild access early; late game centers on the Dark Forest and tracker upgrades.
Full step-by-step and rewards ($500, 10 rifle ammo, 5 painkillers, 1 life stone) are on Tutorial Quests. Difficulty: Easy–medium.
Prerequisite: Zombie tracker level 3 — you cannot enter the Dark Forest until your tracker is at least level 3. Upgrade the tracker at the Hunter's Guild as you earn kills and currency.

Visit the Dark Forest — your first visit also earns the Into the Darkness achievement. Kill a skeleton — mid-tier hunts; tracker level 3+ helps spawns. Kill a witch — same tier band as forest content. Kill a demon — hardest common type; prepare healing and strong weapons. Reach tracker level 5 — guild upgrades; max tier unlocks top detection. Reward: $2000, 5 demon horns, 10 holy water.

Finish The Hunter tutorial quest so you understand hunt pacing and the escape mirror. Farm zombies and lower hunts until you can afford tracker level 3. Enter Dark Forest; prioritize skeleton → witch → demon as encounters appear (results vary by chance). After kills register, bank money and materials for levels 4–5 upgrades. Watch the quest log for milestone updates after each kill and after the final upgrade. Tips: Painkillers and good weapons reduce failed hunts. Use the mirror when a run goes badly. Difficulty: Hard — long grind + tough fights + economy for upgrades.

While hunting you will often unlock milestones such as Hunter Candidate, Amateur Hunter, Professional Hunter, Legendary Hunter, Bone Crusher, Witch Hunter, Demon Fighter, Monster Encyclopedia, Mass Extinction, Into the Darkness, and Getting Serious (max tracker). See Monster Hunter Achievements for a full list and how to earn them.

In Life Simulator Reloaded, quests are multi-step goals tracked in your quest log. Each quest is made of milestones you complete one at a time. Finishing every milestone completes the quest and grants the reward (usually money, items, or both).

Milestones unlock when you perform the matching action (buy an item, win a fight, pass a day in prison, and so on). Some milestones can complete out of order if you already meet the condition when the quest starts. Completed quests stay completed; you cannot repeat them on the same character.

Tutorial line — Core survival and quality-of-life quests often start automatically as you age into young adulthood (typically ages 18–23), guiding market use, jobs, housing, and social goals. Job and module quests — Starting certain jobs (for example beggar) or entering key locations (Hunter's Guild, prison) can auto-start related quests. Childhood — One early quest begins around age 4 and must be finished before age 10.

Rewards are granted once when the final milestone completes. Typical payouts: Cash — scales with difficulty (tutorials → hundreds, master hunter → thousands). Items — consumables, gear, or crafting mats tied to the quest theme. Indirect perks — some quests unlock achievements or gate locations (for example tracker tiers). If you complete milestones but see no reward, verify the entire quest shows as complete; partial progress does not pay out.

Open the quest screen regularly so you know what to do next; rewards often fund the next stage of progression. If a milestone seems stuck, check location, inventory, and job level requirements—many quests assume you are in the right place with the right gear. Difficulty: tutorial quests are easy; long grinds (100 begs, 500 monster kills) are medium–hard mainly due to time. Modules: Crime, Celebrity, and Monster Hunter add their own quest lines on top of core content—buy or enable those modules if a wiki page references them and you do not see the quest.

All three quests start automatically when you enter prison. They can progress in parallel.

Goal: Spend consecutive time locked up on the same sentence — milestones track 10, 20, and 30 days in prison (each day incarcerated counts). Milestone Requirement First stretch 10 days in prison Second stretch 20 days Full run 30 days Reward: $100 when the quest completes. Survival tips Keep health, morale, and energy out of the danger zone — at zero on key stats you can die. Use yard, clinic, food, and legal/social options to stabilize before picking risky fights. Difficulty: Medium if you are new to prison; easy once you learn the daily loop.

Milestones Win three prison fights (wins counted toward this quest). Form a gang — choose Form a Gang: you need strong Prison Reputation, at least two jail friends with friendship at least halfway to the max, then you must win the initiation fight (success adds a few days to your sentence). Reach high standing in prison — the quest talks about 80% prison rep; in practice your Prison Reputation needs to be very high for this step to complete when days pass. Reward: $200. Difficulty: Hard — rep grind + social setup + combat.

Read five books — prison library events and reading actions count toward this (not only the city library). Reach halfway mastery of the Prison Life skill — you passively learn each prison day; books, counseling, and activities speed it up. Reward: $150. Tips: Visit library choices often; pair with low-risk days so you are not constantly in infirmary. Difficulty: Medium.
Core tutorial quests teach market, inventory, employment, housing, monster hunting, and friendships.

Reward: Finishing this quest opens the way for Quality Life once you meet that quest’s requirements. Difficulty: Easy — follow the on-screen milestones.

Goal: Move from surviving to stable independence. Get promoted at your job. Rent a house. Buy a home decoration item. Place that item in your home. Reward: Includes $500 and meal items in-game. Difficulty: Easy — requires income and housing flow.
Goal: Build meaningful friendships (follow the in-game quest text — talk, hang out, and deepen relationships). Reward: $2000 on full completion. Difficulty: Medium — needs social actions and time.

Combat-oriented skills decide how hard you hit in brawls, how athletic actions feel, and how effective ranged hunting gear is. All three are worth raising if you touch crime, prison, or the Monster Hunter module. None of these skills replace health management—carry heals for bad streaks.

Fighting is the backbone of unarmed and melee-style confrontations: street fights, prison brawls, prison attack options, and the monster punch attack in hunts. It levels from winning engagements and from dedicated training loops (gym work, prison fight training, and similar repeated combat practice).

Sports supports general athletic performance. Train it at the gym, through sports-flavored training actions, and via moves like the prison kick attack. It also combines with fighting in some damage formulas—do not neglect it if you rely on punching your way out of problems.

Aiming controls rifle damage in monster hunts (higher skill widens the damage range toward the top end) and improves consistency with ranged combat. You train it by shooting the rifle (chance per shot) and by dagger-related hunting practice. Pair it with ammo stock and a maintained rifle—see Hunting items. tip If you only hunt occasionally, still fire the rifle when safe fights appear: aiming is slow to grow without live shots. For prison-heavy runs, fighting + sports matter more than aiming.
Skills overview Professional skills Exact gain rates can vary by action; use repeated, on-theme activities to grind reliably.

In Life Simulator Reloaded, skills are long-term proficiencies that gate jobs, fights, crimes, social checks, and module content (prison, celebrity, monster hunting). Each skill has a maximum level; you raise it by repeating relevant actions, jobs, education, and usable items.

Every point of intelligence adds +0.002 to the progress you gain toward skills when you learn. Over a long life, a smart character levels professional and combat skills noticeably faster than a low-intelligence one—plan stats if you are aiming for a specialist build.

Honor and evil are a moral axis pair: crime-heavy play pushes evil, while lawful or virtuous choices push honor. They cap each other narratively and mechanically as opposites—leaning into one path often means the other stays lower. Use this when deciding whether a run is a hero, antihero, or full outlaw.

Social skills shape dialogue outcomes, job advancement, service careers, and how you weather stress. They are often the difference between a promotion, a failed negotiation, or a calm exit from a bad event.
Used heavily in social decisions and negotiations—anything where you talk someone into (or out of) an outcome. Invest here if you like relationship-heavy play or want safer rolls on charm checks.
Leadership feeds job promotions and management tracks. If you are climbing from line work into supervisory roles, keep this skill rising alongside job-specific skills.
Powers social interactions and customer-facing work such as bartending and waitressing. It is a workhorse for service careers and general likability checks.
The moral side of the axis: lawful, generous, or upright choices push honor. It is the counter-skill to evil—high honor runs feel like “clean” lives; it also gates some positive social outcomes.

Crime-related actions and ruthless decisions raise evil. It is the counter to honor and supports darker paths (theft, violence, intimidation). Expect tension between honor and evil on a single character.

Helps in stress situations: high-pressure jobs, danger, or events that test nerves. Pair with decent morale recovery habits so you are not always one bad day from a spiral. tip Pick a social identity early: high honor + persuasion for “clean talker,” or evil + calmness for a cold criminal. Mixing extremes works but slows both axes compared to committing to one story. Many social checks also look at relationships and context; skills raise your odds, not guaranteed wins.

Interactions are per-person actions (handshake-style options in the UI). They depend on relationship category (family, romance, friends, coworkers, jail), your friendship, love, and hate with that person, and sometimes location or how many times you can use them per day.

Category Typical interactions Family Support, gifts, working through conflict Romance Dates, intimacy, commitment beats Friends Hangouts, favors, introductions Coworkers Office-style socializing — can grow into real friendship Jail Prison-only set (needs the crime pack and an active sentence) Effects usually change friendship, love, hate, and sometimes money, morale, or skills.

You must be in prison and the person must be in the jail relationship group unless the game says otherwise. Interaction Effect summary Greet +3 friendship, +2 prison reputation (limited once per day) Intimidate If prison reputation ≥ 60: +3 reputation, +10 hate and −5 friendship on the target. Otherwise you trigger a standard prison fight (often +2 days on your sentence on a typical outcome) Trade Needs ≥ 30 friendship; +3 friendship, +$5–20 Share meal +10 friendship, −5 energy Gossip +5 friendship, +3 prison life skill Ask protection Needs ≥ 50 friendship; −3 friendship, +5 prison life (up to 3 times per day) Fight Easier or tougher opponent depending on hate; win/lose follows prison fight rules Defend friend Needs ≥ 60 friendship; prison fight — on a win: +20 friendship, +5 reputation, +2 days, plus an achievement Steal Success chance scales with prison life and fighting (capped); success gives money; failure costs −20 friendship, +20 hate, often +2 days Extort Needs prison reputation ≥ 120; chance based on your rep vs their hate; success gives money and hate; failure often +3 days Recruit Needs an active gang and ≥ 40 friendship; adds a member, +15 friendship, +3 reputation Bribe guard Costs 5 gems; 50% chance to shave 5 sentence days or +30 friendship with that guard aviso Failed prison interactions often reset your “clean record” streak for reports and the 7-day good-behavior check — the game tracks your last trouble day for that.

Greet and gossip early for safe reputation and friendship. Intimidate only when your reputation is high enough to avoid the forced brawl (≥ 60). Extort is late-game bullying — huge reputation requirement and a harsh failure state. For bonds outside prison, see Relationships guide and Mechanics: relationships.

Every NPC has friendship, love, and hate (and other flags) grouped by relationship type (family, romance, friends, work, jail, and so on). Gameplay is about moving those numbers over time — not a single branching dialogue tree.

Lever What to do Consistency Interact daily when limits allow; many actions are capped per day Alignment Pick story choices that fit the situation (work vs home, and so on) Gifts and activities Use location actions (parks, restaurants) that explicitly help relationships Avoid hate spikes High hate unlocks sabotage and fights; recover with apologies or space tip Coworkers can become friends after enough positive socializing — great for job stability and social invites.

Family ties help early stability: They respond to support interactions and shared events Letters from prison can randomly raise a family member’s friendship (+5) when you write from a cell or library Deaths, divorces, and rivalries still come from base-game random events Keep morale up so you have energy to maintain family during grindy jobs.

Romantic arcs use the romance category: Raise love and friendship through flirt and date style beats (exact options vary by age and location). Watch for blockers — existing partners, age limits, or conflicting story situations. When commitment choices appear, decide carefully; saying no often has a cost. info Love and friendship are separate meters. You can be close friends without romance, or romantic while fixing hate after a fight — know which bar you are working on.

Stabilize income first — weddings and housing strain money. Raise friendship before proposals if the game checks trust; some beats fail if you rush. After marriage, keep showing up with positive interactions; neglect can push hate up in some event pools. aviso Big negative swings (cheating beats, crime coming to light) can crash several meters at once. Keep gems in mind for damage-control choices if you play risky. For category definitions, see Mechanics: relationships.
